source: Jonathan Grimm's hand-drawn master timeline (kraft paper, photographed October 2026)
quotes: Retirement has been an idea that is years in the making.
Inception. An idea… the most resilient parasite.
You need the simplest version of the idea.
Perhaps… you will not want to see…
Elephants… You know the genesis… Get an idea deep enough.

1.hand: Civil War 1861–1865 → seed: Segregation / Boundaries. (1935: “Not for all”)

6.hand: Market → Speculative · Opportunity · Possibility · Speed → Get Rich Quick. Seed so rooted in our humanity.

7.hand: Black Tuesday · Great Depression 1929–39 → seed: 2 Americas (rich / rural)

matches.hand: 1935 Social Security Act ← Not for all · 65/Old · Gov’t
GI Bill. Often state admin of benefits. Racial seg states did not get $ owed housing + other.

add.title: The Dutch East India Company sells the first public shares
add.detail: In 1602 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) raised its capital by selling shares to the public in Amsterdam, and those shares traded on what became the world’s first stock exchange.
add.significance: Owning a slice of a company’s future profits begins here, the instrument the 401(k) era would later ask workers to retire on.
add.hand: Market (stock market) — East India Trade Co: first stock

add.title: Tulip mania
add.detail: Prices for rare tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic rose to extraordinary levels in 1636 and collapsed in February 1637. Historians still debate how widespread the losses were.
add.significance: The archetype of a speculative bubble: the Get Rich Quick impulse centuries before anyone held a retirement account.

add.title: The Industrial Revolution
add.detail: Beginning in Britain around 1760 and reaching the United States in the early 1800s, mechanized production moved work from farms and workshops into factories and wage labor.
add.significance: Farm to factory: the change that turned growing old from a shift in role into a loss of income, the problem retirement was later invented to manage.
add.hand: 1760–1840 Industrial Revolution. Farm to factory. Climax of ideas + tech. Transformation of labor + economy.

add.title: Independence
add.detail: The Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776. That same year the Continental Congress promised half pay to soldiers disabled in the war, the first American public pension.

add.title: The Buttonwood Agreement founds the New York Stock Exchange
add.detail: On May 17, 1792, 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement on Wall Street, the origin of the New York Stock Exchange.
add.significance: The marketplace where American retirement savings would eventually be invested.

add.title: Edison’s practical light bulb
add.detail: Thomas Edison’s laboratory demonstrated a long-lasting incandescent lamp in 1879. Electric light and power spread over the next half century.
add.significance: The start of electrification, which would remake factory work and the pace of industrial life.

add.title: Electric motors drive about 5% of factory machinery
add.detail: Electric motors supplied less than 5 percent of the power used to drive machinery in U.S. manufacturing in 1899, and more than half by 1919 (Devine, 1983).
add.significance: Electrification raised factory productivity and the pace of work, part of what pushed older industrial workers out.

add.title: The Wright brothers fly
add.detail: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered, controlled airplane flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903.

add.title: About 8% of homes have electricity
add.detail: About 8 percent of U.S. homes had electric service in 1907. By 1920 about 35 percent did.

add.title: Ford’s Model T
add.detail: Introduced October 1, 1908, the Model T put a car within reach of ordinary families. Ford’s moving assembly line followed in 1913.
add.significance: His question on the timeline: what does this do to travel and to the move from farm to factory?
add.hand: 1908 Model T. What does this do to travel + farm → factory dynamics?

add.title: About a third of homes are electrified
add.detail: About 35 percent of U.S. homes had electricity in 1920.

add.title: The Great Depression
add.detail: From the 1929 crash through the end of the decade, output and prices collapsed, thousands of banks failed, and unemployment reached about 25 percent in 1933.
add.significance: Pulled both Americas into the same reckoning and made Social Security politically possible.

add.title: Two-thirds of homes are electrified, rural America is not
add.detail: By 1930 roughly two-thirds of U.S. homes had electricity, but only about a quarter of rural residents did. The Rural Electrification Administration was created in 1935 to close the gap.
add.significance: Two Americas in one statistic: the cities wired, the countryside waiting.

add.title: National Housing Act creates the FHA
add.detail: Signed June 27, 1934, the act created the Federal Housing Administration to insure home mortgages. FHA underwriting treated racial mixing as a risk to property values: its 1938 manual told appraisers to check whether “incompatible racial and social groups are present” and said neighborhoods should stay “occupied by the same social and racial classes.” A sister agency, the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (1933), drew the color-coded maps that gave redlining its name.
add.significance: Home equity became the second pillar of middle-class retirement, and federal policy rationed it by race for a generation. The effects on family wealth outlived the rules.
add.hand: ’33 / ’34 FHA created. REDLINING. Housing shortage led to FHA. FHA → mandated segregation for new housing.

add.title: The Arroyo Seco Parkway, the first freeway in the West
add.detail: Dedicated December 30, 1940, between Los Angeles and Pasadena, it was California’s first freeway.
add.significance: The car-and-freeway geography of the postwar suburbs, where much of the golden age’s home equity was built, starts here.

add.title: World War II
add.detail: War began in Europe in September 1939. The United States entered after the attack on Pearl Harbor and fought until Japan’s surrender in 1945.
add.significance: Full employment, wage controls and the push for employer pensions. The generation that fought it built the golden age of retirement.

add.title: Pearl Harbor
add.detail: Japan attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, and the United States entered the war.

add.title: The atomic bomb
add.detail: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, and Japan surrendered weeks later.
add.significance: The book’s Crucible chapter places it among the shocks the 1950 sixty-year-old carried into retirement.

add.title: The Cold War
add.detail: A four-decade rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, from the Truman Doctrine in 1947 to the Soviet collapse in 1991.
add.significance: The book describes postwar anxiety and abundance as roommates; that mood made a secure retirement feel like the reward.

add.title: Brown v. Board of Education
add.detail: On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court ruled that state-mandated segregation of public schools violates the Fourteenth Amendment.
add.significance: Education is now one of the strongest predictors of household wealth. Who could attend which schools shaped who would later retire securely.

add.title: The civil rights movement
add.detail: From the Montgomery bus boycott to the Civil Rights, Voting Rights and Fair Housing Acts, a mass movement dismantled legal segregation.
add.significance: Won formal equality, while systems built on earlier exclusions, in housing and in retirement, kept compounding.

add.title: Sputnik and the space race
add.detail: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, on October 4, 1957.

add.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
add.detail: In October 1962 the United States and the Soviet Union came to the brink of nuclear war over Soviet missiles in Cuba.

add.title: Equal Pay Act
add.detail: Signed June 10, 1963, the act required equal pay for women and men doing substantially equal work in the same workplace.
add.significance: Wages drive savings, pensions and Social Security benefits. A pay gap becomes a retirement gap.

add.title: President Kennedy is assassinated
add.detail: John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas on November 22, 1963.

add.title: The Beatles era
add.detail: The Beatles’ February 1964 appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show set off Beatlemania in the United States. The band broke up in 1970.

add.title: The Vietnam War
add.detail: U.S. combat troops arrived in Vietnam in 1965 and the last left in 1973. Saigon fell in 1975.
add.significance: The Climax chapter names Vietnam and Watergate as what corroded the institutional trust that collective promises depend on.

add.title: The Summer of Love
add.detail: In 1967 tens of thousands of young people gathered in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury, the high point of the counterculture.

add.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated
add.detail: King was assassinated in Memphis on April 4, 1968. Congress passed the Fair Housing Act a week later.

add.title: Fair Housing Act
add.detail: Signed April 11, 1968, Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 banned discrimination in the sale, rental and financing of housing.
add.significance: Outlawed redlining going forward, but could not return the decades of home equity families had been denied.
add.hand: ’68 Fair Housing Act to end REDLINING

add.title: The Moon landing
add.detail: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
add.significance: A high point of postwar confidence in what large institutions could do.

add.title: Watergate
add.detail: The June 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee’s offices led to President Nixon’s resignation on August 9, 1974.
add.significance: With Vietnam, the book’s example of trust in institutions eroding just as retirement depended on it.

add.title: Equal Credit Opportunity Act
add.detail: Signed October 28, 1974, and effective in 1975, the act barred lenders from discriminating on the basis of sex or marital status; 1976 amendments added race, color, religion, national origin and age. Before it, lenders often refused women credit in their own names or required a husband’s signature.
add.significance: Credit in your own name comes before owning a home or a business, two of the main ways families build wealth for later life.
add.hand: Equal Credit Opportunity Act. Women get the right to have bank acct + credit + loans w/o male co-signer.

add.title: Microsoft is founded
add.detail: Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft on April 4, 1975.

add.title: Apple Computer is founded
add.detail: Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne founded Apple Computer on April 1, 1976.

add.title: Community Reinvestment Act
add.detail: Signed October 12, 1977, the act requires federal regulators to assess whether banks meet the credit needs of their whole communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
add.significance: The third step in the redlining thread: from drawing the lines (1930s), to banning them (1968), to requiring lending inside them (1977).

add.title: Iran, the energy crisis and the early-1980s recession
add.detail: The Iranian Revolution sent oil prices soaring in 1979. To break double-digit inflation the Federal Reserve pushed interest rates to record highs (the prime rate reached 21.5 percent), and unemployment hit 10.8 percent in late 1982, the highest since the Great Depression.
add.significance: High rates and inflation strained pensions and household budgets just as the 401(k) arrived.
add.hand: Iran · Energy crisis ’79–’82 · High % rate → Worst recession since Great Depression. ↑ Unemploy · ↑ Inflation · Global crisis.

add.title: Bank deregulation (DIDMCA)
add.detail: Signed March 31, 1980, the Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act began phasing out federal ceilings on the interest banks could pay depositors (Regulation Q).
add.significance: Opened the competition for savers’ money that market-based retirement products would win.

add.title: Women’s Business Ownership Act
add.detail: Signed October 25, 1988, the act ended the need for a husband or male relative to co-sign a woman’s business loan, and created the Women’s Business Center program and the National Women’s Business Council.
add.significance: Business ownership is a path to wealth outside the paycheck-and-pension track.
add.hand: Women can get business loan w/o male co-signer. Business Ownership Act.

add.title: CNBC launches
add.detail: CNBC began broadcasting on April 17, 1989, bringing all-day business news and live market prices into living rooms.
add.significance: Money becomes television: fuel for both the Market Growth and Get Rich Quick seeds.

add.title: The Gulf War
add.detail: Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990. A U.S.-led coalition drove Iraqi forces out by the end of February 1991.

add.title: The end of the Soviet Union
add.detail: The Soviet Union dissolved on December 26, 1991, ending the Cold War.
add.significance: Market capitalism without a rival, the backdrop for the 1990s’ faith in markets.

add.title: The World Wide Web goes public
add.detail: Tim Berners-Lee’s World Wide Web became publicly available in August 1991, and CERN released it royalty-free in April 1993.

add.title: The Los Angeles riots
add.detail: The March 1991 police beating of Rodney King was caught on video. The acquittal of the officers in April 1992 set off days of unrest in Los Angeles.

add.title: The World Trade Center truck bombing
add.detail: A truck bomb exploded beneath the North Tower of the World Trade Center on February 26, 1993, killing six people.

add.title: The Waco siege
add.detail: A 51-day standoff between federal agents and the Branch Davidians near Waco, Texas, ended in a fire on April 19, 1993.

add.title: “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell”
add.detail: The 1993 policy barred openly gay, lesbian and bisexual people from military service while ending questioning about orientation. It was repealed in 2011.

add.title: Amazon is founded
add.detail: Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in July 1994 as an online bookstore.

add.title: The Oklahoma City bombing
add.detail: A truck bomb destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.

add.title: The O.J. Simpson trial
add.detail: The televised murder trial of O.J. Simpson ended in an acquittal on October 3, 1995, one of the most-watched events of the decade.

add.title: The Asian financial crisis reaches Wall Street
add.detail: Currency collapses that began in Thailand in July 1997 spread across East Asia. On October 27 the Dow fell 554 points, and market-wide circuit breakers halted U.S. trading for the first time.
add.significance: A “mini panic” the long bull market quickly absorbed, teaching a generation of 401(k) savers that dips are buying opportunities.

add.title: The Lewinsky scandal
add.detail: The scandal broke in January 1998. The House impeached President Clinton that December, and the Senate acquitted him in February 1999.

add.title: Russia defaults; Long-Term Capital Management fails
add.detail: In August 1998 Russia devalued the ruble and defaulted on its domestic debt. The losses helped topple the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, and the New York Fed organized a private rescue in September.
add.significance: Another sharp scare that recovered within months, reinforcing faith in buying and holding.

add.title: The Dow closes above 10,000
add.detail: On March 29, 1999, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 10,000 for the first time.
add.significance: A headline number that made the market feel like a reliable escalator.

add.title: Columbine
add.detail: On April 20, 1999, two students killed 13 people at Columbine High School in Colorado.

add.title: Y2K
add.detail: Fear that computers would fail when dates rolled over to 2000 prompted a costly worldwide fix. The new year arrived with few problems.

add.title: September 11
add.detail: Terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, at the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania. U.S. stock markets closed for four trading days.
add.significance: His note: social, political and economic at once. It struck in the middle of the dot-com bear market.

add.title: The COVID-19 pandemic
add.detail: The World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic on March 11, 2020. More than 1.1 million Americans died of it.
add.significance: He pairs it with 1918, “the original COVID-19.” Both pandemics reshaped work and family; this one also pushed a wave of older workers into early retirement.

add.title: The fight over fair access to banking
add.detail: In January 2021 the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a “fair access” rule requiring large banks to judge customers individually rather than refusing whole categories of lawful business; it was paused weeks later. Fair Access to Banking Act bills were reintroduced in Congress in 2025, and an August 7, 2025, executive order directed regulators to act against politicized “debanking.”
add.significance: The newest chapter in a long argument over who gets access to financial services, and on what terms.
add.hand: Fair Access to Fin. Serv. Act

notes.detail: The 1890s: industry overtakes the farm, and the idea of an age to stop working begins to take hold.
Electric power, the automobile and powered flight all arrive within a decade.
Consumer abundance, buying on margin and the first mass stock market: three seeds (Market, Leisure, Get Rich Quick) planted at once.
The postwar decades when the middle class grew fastest. The Climax chapter calls them an unrepeatable anomaly.
The three sources meant to carry retirement: Social Security, an employer pension and personal savings. His seed note adds: “for some…”
The Collapse chapter returns to these chains as a “you’re supposed to” one generation built and the next quietly refused.

notes.text: Market prominence: individuals in · new Roaring 20’s · retirement accts · wild west · movies!
notes.detail: Markets move to the center of ordinary financial life.
His note on the long bull market. For reference, the S&P 500 rose from 102.42 (Aug. 12, 1982) to 1,527.46 (Mar. 24, 2000), about 16.6% a year in price alone.
An industry grew up to manage the transfer of retirement risk from employers to individuals, the Codify chapter’s “game” and “industry.”
The book’s central question for the Codify era: was the golden age a model to copy, or an anomaly that could not be repeated?

notes.text: All 9 seeds in full bloom · Personal finance
notes.detail: By the turn of the century every one of the nine seeds is in full bloom, and retirement has become “personal finance.”
His note on the market between the dot-com crash and the 2008 crisis.

threads.title: Redlining: drawn, banned, still felt
threads.summary: He underlined redlining in red three times: federal policy drew the lines in the 1930s, Congress banned them in 1968, and in 1977 required banks to lend inside them. The rules changed; the wealth gap they created kept compounding.

threads.title: Money in your own name
threads.summary: Equal pay (1963), credit without a husband’s signature (1974), business loans without a male co-signer (1988), and the current fight over fair access to banking: each step widened who could build wealth in their own name.
